passages.p1:
Eight persons A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a square table. Four of them sit at the corners and face outside; the other four sit in the middle of the sides and face the centre. Seats are counted one after another around the table, and 'left' and 'right' are taken from each person's own point of view.
A sits in the middle of a side. B sits second to the left of A. C sits immediate right of B. D sits at a corner. E sits opposite D. F sits immediate left of E. G sits third to the right of C.
passages.p2:
A machine rearranges a set of numbers step by step. An illustration of an input and its steps is given below.
Input: 56 23 89 34 71 18
Step I: 18 56 23 89 34 71
Step II: 18 89 56 23 34 71
Step III: 18 89 23 56 34 71
Step IV: 18 89 23 71 56 34
Step V: 18 89 23 71 34 56
Step V is the last step of this input.
Study the rule and answer the questions for the following new input:
40 15 72 29 63 8 51

questions.text:
What should come in place of the question mark?

3, 5, 11, 29, 83, ?
questions.explanation: The gaps are 2, 6, 18, 54, each three times the one before, so the next gap is 162 and the term is 83 + 162 = 245.
questions.trap: Using a doubling gap instead of a tripling gap.
questions.revise: Series with gaps in geometric progression

questions.text:
What should come in place of the question mark?

11, 12, 16, 25, 41, ?
questions.explanation: The gaps are 1², 2², 3², 4², and the next gap is 5² = 25. So 41 + 25 = 66.
questions.trap: Picking the next square as the term instead of the next gap.
wrongReasons: Took the next square, 64, as the term

questions.text:
Select the option that will come next in the series.

ZAB, XCE, UFI, QJN, ?
questions.explanation: First letters Z, X, U, Q move −2, −3, −4, so the next move is −5: Q → L. Second letters A, C, F, J move +2, +3, +4, so the next is +5: J → O. Third letters B, E, I, N move +3, +4, +5, so the next is +6: N → T.
steps: First letters: −2, −3, −4, next −5: L
Second letters: +2, +3, +4, next +5: O
Third letters: +3, +4, +5, next +6: T
LOT
questions.trap: Moving the first letter forward instead of backward.
questions.shortcut: Handle each letter position as a separate series.

questions.text:
Select the number that is related to the third number in the same way as the second number is related to the first number.

7 : 336 :: 5 : ?
steps: Rule: n(n² − 1) = n³ − n
questions.trap: Using n³ and forgetting to subtract n.
questions.shortcut: 336 is close to 7³ = 343; the difference is 7.

steps: Spot what the question tests: Water image = top-bottom swap.
Option A (Figure A) is out: This is the left-right mirror image.
Option C (Figure C) is out: This is a rotation.
Option D (Figure D) is out: This is both flips, i.e. a 180° rotation.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing the left-right inversion.
So the answer is option B: Figure B.
questions.trap: Choosing the left-right inversion.

questions.text: In a certain code language, STUDENT is written as TSVCFMU. How will PLANET be written in that code?
questions.explanation: STUDENT → TSVCFMU alternates +1 and −1 starting with +1. For PLANET: P+1 = Q, L−1 = K, A+1 = B, N−1 = M, E+1 = F, T−1 = S.
steps: Apply the same pattern to PLANET
QKBMFS
questions.trap: Using +1 for every letter.
questions.shortcut: Check the first two letters: the pair of shifts decides the pattern.

questions.text: In a certain code language, CAT is written as 24 and DOG is written as 26. How will BIRD be written in that code?
questions.explanation: The code is the sum of the alphabet positions: CAT = 3 + 1 + 20 = 24 and DOG = 4 + 15 + 7 = 26. BIRD = 2 + 9 + 18 + 4 = 33.
questions.trap: Slipping on one position value.

steps: Spot what the question tests: Fold line = mirror line for punched holes.
Option B (Figure B) is out: Only two holes: it misses the second fold.
Option C (Figure C) is out: Only two holes on a diagonal, which ignores one fold.
Option D (Figure D) is out: Has a stray hole at the centre and a missing quarter.
Common slip to avoid: Forgetting that two folds give four holes, or placing the extra holes diagonally only.
So the answer is option A: Figure A.

questions.revise: Fold line = mirror line for punched holes
wrongReasons: Only two holes: it misses the second fold

questions.text: Rahul starts from his house and walks 9 km towards the west. He turns left and walks 12 km, turns left again and walks 3 km, and finally turns left and walks 4 km. How far and in which direction is he from his house?
questions.explanation: West 9: (−9, 0). Left from west is south: 12 km to (−9, −12). Left from south is east: 3 km to (−6, −12). Left from east is north: 4 km to (−6, −8). Distance = √(6² + 8²) = 10 km, towards the south-west.
steps: Left → south 12: (−9, −12)
Left → east 3: (−6, −12)
Left → north 4: (−6, −8)
√(36 + 64) = 10 km, South-West
questions.trap: Adding 6 and 8 instead of using Pythagoras.
questions.revise: Turns relative to the direction faced
wrongReasons: Added the net distances instead of using Pythagoras

questions.text: In a row of 40 boys, Arjun is 13th from the left and Bhanu is 17th from the right. How many boys are there between them?
questions.explanation: Bhanu is 40 − 17 + 1 = 24th from the left. Boys between positions 13 and 24 = 24 − 13 − 1 = 10.
steps: Bhanu from left = 40 − 17 + 1 = 24
questions.trap: Forgetting the +1 when converting the rank.
wrongReasons: Subtracted the ranks without removing both positions
Added the two ranks and removed 16

questions.text:
Statements:
No lock is a key.
All keys are doors.
Some doors are windows.

Conclusions:
I. Some doors are not locks.
II. Some windows are not locks.
III. No key is a lock.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: All I, II and III follow
questions.explanation: Keys are doors and no key is a lock, so some doors (the keys) are not locks (I). 'No lock is a key' converts to 'No key is a lock' (III). The windows that are doors may or may not be keys, so II is only a possibility.
steps: All keys are doors; no key is a lock: some doors are not locks (I)
Converse of 'No lock is a key': no key is a lock (III)
Windows may be locks or not: II is not certain
questions.trap: Treating a possibility as a definite conclusion.
wrongReasons: III also follows: it is the converse of the first statement
questions.approach: Check the converse of every 'no' and 'some' statement first.

questions.explanation: All poets are writers, so P lies inside W. Some teachers are writers and some may be poets, so T overlaps both W and P.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Venn: subset, overlap, disjoint.
Option A (Figure A) is out: Poets sits outside writers, which is false.
Option B (Figure B) is out: Poets and teachers are swapped.
Option C (Figure C) is out: Writers, poets and teachers are drawn as separate sets.
Common slip to avoid: Drawing teachers as separate from poets.
So the answer is option D: Figure D.
questions.trap: Drawing teachers as separate from poets.
wrongReasons: Poets sits outside writers, which is false
Writers, poets and teachers are drawn as separate sets

questions.text: If 18 July 2026 is a Saturday, on which day of the week was 3 March 2026?
questions.explanation: From 3 March to 18 July is 28 + 30 + 31 + 30 + 18 = 137 days. 137 = 19 weeks + 4 days, so 3 March was 4 days before a Saturday: Tuesday.
steps: Days left in March after the 3rd: 28
April 30, May 31, June 30, July 18
Saturday − 4 = Tuesday
questions.trap: Counting March as having 31 days from the 3rd.

questions.text: A clock gains 5 minutes every hour. It is set right at 6 a.m. What time will it show at the true time of 12 noon?
questions.explanation: In 6 true hours the clock gains 6 × 5 = 30 minutes. At the true time of 12 noon it shows 12:30 p.m.
steps: True time elapsed = 6 hours
Gain = 6 × 5 = 30 minutes
Clock shows 12:30 p.m.
questions.trap: Adding the hourly gain only once.
questions.revise: Clocks that gain or lose time

questions.text:
Three persons P, Q and R sit in a row facing north. Who sits in the middle?

I. P sits to the right of R.
II. Q does not sit at the extreme left end.
options: Both statements together are not sufficient
questions.explanation: From I, the possible orders (left to right) are R-P-Q, R-Q-P and Q-R-P. Statement II removes Q-R-P, but R-P-Q and R-Q-P remain, so the middle person is P or Q.
steps: I: R is left of P: RPQ, RQP, QRP
II: Q not at the left end: removes QRP
RPQ and RQP remain: middle is P or Q
Not sufficient
questions.trap: Assuming the two clues together fix a single order.
wrongReasons: Q could still be in the middle or at an end
R and P are not placed
R P Q and R Q P are both possible
questions.approach: List every arrangement allowed by each statement and combine them.

questions.text: Who sits immediate right of H?
questions.explanation: Going clockwise: E, A, C, B, D, G, H, F (E, C, D and H at the corners). H sits at a corner and faces outside, so H's right is the next seat clockwise, which is F.
steps: Place A in the middle of a side; B is second to its left (A faces the centre, so left is clockwise): B is 2 seats clockwise of A
C is immediate right of B: C is the corner between A and B
D at a corner, E opposite D: E is the corner before A
F is immediate left of E (E faces outside, so left is anticlockwise): F sits before E
G is third to the right of C: G sits between D and H
Clockwise order: E, A, C, B, D, G, H, F
H faces outside, right is clockwise: F
questions.trap: Using the facing-centre rule for a person at a corner.
wrongReasons: G sits immediate left of H

steps: Spot what the question tests: Dice: a face never appears together with its opposite.
Option A (5) is out: 5 is next to 1 in the first view.

Option C (2) is out: 2 is never visible, so it cannot be fixed by these views.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing 5, which is next to 1 in the first view.
So the answer is option D: 6.
